chapter.title: Data Models and Query Languages
chapter.author: Martin Kleppmann
chapter.primary_goal: Understand how relational, document, and graph data models represent relationships, how their query languages shape application design, and why the right model depends on the application's data.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 2 argues that data models profoundly shape both software structure and how engineers think about a problem. Applications are built as layers of representation: real-world concepts become application objects, those objects become relational tables, documents, or graphs, those models become bytes, and eventually hardware representations. The chapter compares relational and document models, showing that document databases fit self-contained tree-shaped data well, while relational databases handle many-to-one and many-to-many relationships more naturally through references and joins. It traces this tradeoff back to hierarchical databases, CODASYL's network model, and the relational model's decision to remove application-managed access paths in favor of declarative queries and query optimizers. It then compares schema-on-read with schema-on-write, discusses document locality and its limits, and observes that relational and document systems are converging. The query-language section contrasts imperative programming with declarative SQL, CSS, and XPath/XSL, emphasizing that declarative languages hide execution details and allow optimization and parallelization. MapReduce is presented as an intermediate model between declarative and imperative querying, with pure map/reduce functions enabling distributed execution. The final major section covers graph-shaped data: property graphs, Cypher, recursive SQL, triple-stores, RDF, SPARQL, and Datalog. The chapter's central conclusion is that document, relational, and graph models are all useful in different domains; trying to force one model into another is possible but often awkward.

Explain the motivations behind NoSQL adoption and polyglot persistence.
Explain the object-relational impedance mismatch and the limits of ORMs.
Compare normalized relational and JSON representations of a one-to-many résumé/profile.
Explain why IDs and normalization reduce duplication and inconsistency.
Explain why many-to-one and many-to-many relationships challenge document models.
Compare the hierarchical, network/CODASYL, and relational models historically.
Explain access paths in CODASYL and why they made application code inflexible.
Explain how relational query optimizers replaced application-managed access paths.
Compare document and relational models for application-code simplicity.
Distinguish schema-on-read and schema-on-write.
Explain when schema flexibility is useful and when explicit schemas are beneficial.
Explain document data locality, including its benefits and performance limitations.
Explain the convergence of relational and document databases.

Use CSS/XPath as analogies for declarative data querying.
Explain MapReduce's map/reduce execution model and purity restrictions.
Explain why MongoDB introduced the aggregation pipeline in addition to MapReduce.

layers.representation: Real-world people, organizations, goods, actions, money, sensors, etc. become application objects/data structures and APIs.
Application structures are expressed in a general-purpose model such as JSON/XML documents, relational tables, or graphs.
Database engines encode the chosen data model into bytes in memory, on disk, or on the network.
Hardware represents bytes using electrical currents, light pulses, magnetic fields, and other physical mechanisms.

data_model_layering.main_point: Each layer hides lower-level complexity behind a cleaner data model, enabling different groups of engineers to work independently.
data_model_layering.model_assumptions: Every data model makes some operations natural or fast and others awkward, slow, or unsupported.

relational_model.structure: Data is organized into relations/tables, each an unordered collection of tuples/rows.
relational_model.key_idea: Hide physical/internal data representation behind a clean logical interface.
relational_model.historical_outcome: By the mid-1980s relational databases and SQL became dominant and generalized well beyond their initial business-processing use cases.

nosql.name_origin: NoSQL originally appeared as a Twitter hashtag for a 2009 meetup about open-source, distributed, nonrelational databases; it was later reinterpreted as 'Not Only SQL.'
drivers: Need for scale beyond what relational systems could easily achieve, including huge datasets or high write throughput.
Specialized query operations poorly supported by the relational model.
Frustration with rigid relational schemas and desire for more dynamic/expressive models.
nosql.polyglot_persistence: Relational and nonrelational databases are likely to coexist because different applications have different requirements.

object_relational_mismatch.definition: The awkward translation between object-oriented application data structures and relational tables, rows, and columns.
object_relational_mismatch.orm_limit: ORMs reduce boilerplate but cannot fully hide differences between object and relational models.

linkedin_profile.relational_approach: Put repeated child collections in separate tables with foreign keys to users.
linkedin_profile.document_approach: Store the profile as one self-contained JSON document.
linkedin_profile.document_locality_advantage: A profile can be fetched in one query because related one-to-many data is co-located.

normalization_and_relationships.id_property: A database ID has no human meaning and therefore can remain stable even if the human-readable information changes.
normalization_and_relationships.normalization: Removing duplication by storing a human-meaningful fact once and referring to it by ID, reducing update overhead and inconsistency risk.
normalization_and_relationships.document_model_problem: Normalization creates many-to-one references, and growing application features often create many-to-many relationships. These require joins or application-managed follow-up queries, which document databases may handle poorly.

hierarchical_model.structure: Tree of records nested inside records; every record has exactly one parent.
hierarchical_model.weakness: Poor for many-to-many relationships and no joins.
hierarchical_model.similarity_to_documents: Strong resemblance to nested JSON/document databases.

network_model_codasyL.structure: Generalized hierarchy where a record can have multiple parents.
network_model_codasyL.relationship_links: Disk-stored pointer-like links rather than relational foreign keys.
network_model_codasyL.access_path: Applications traverse predefined paths through links/cursors to reach records.
network_model_codasyL.problem: Application developers had to understand and maintain all access paths. Changing paths could require rewriting large amounts of query code, making the data model difficult to evolve.

relational_response.structure: Expose tables as simple sets of rows without application-visible navigation paths.
relational_response.query_optimizer: The database optimizer chooses indexes, join strategies, and execution order automatically.
relational_response.benefit: New indexes and new query patterns can often be added without rewriting application queries around new access paths.

document_strengths: Closer match to application structures for tree-shaped one-to-many data

guidance.document_model: Best fit when data is document-like/tree-shaped and generally loaded as a whole.
guidance.relational_model: Usually better for connected data requiring many joins and references.
guidance.graph_model: Most natural when data is highly interconnected.

document_vs_relational_today.denormalization_tradeoff: Denormalization can avoid joins but moves consistency-maintenance work into application code.

schema_on_read.definition: Structure is implicit and interpreted by application code when data is read.

schema_on_write.definition: Schema is explicit and the database validates written data against it.

migration_example.change: Split a single name field into first_name and last_name.
migration_example.document_strategy: Start writing new fields and let read code handle older documents.
migration_example.relational_strategy: ALTER TABLE to add fields, then potentially UPDATE existing rows.
migration_example.important_nuance: ALTER TABLE is fast in many relational databases, but rewriting all rows with UPDATE can be expensive; an application may also fill missing fields at read time.

schema_on_read_good_for: Data shaped by external systems that may change unpredictably
schema_flexibility.schema_on_write_good_for: Collections where records are expected to share the same structure and the schema is useful for documentation/enforcement.

data_locality.benefit: A document stored as one contiguous JSON/XML/BSON object can be efficient when the application usually reads most or all of it.
costs: The entire document may need loading even if only a small field is needed.
Updates often require rewriting the entire document.
data_locality.recommendation: Keep documents fairly small and avoid writes that significantly increase their size.

model_convergence.relational_direction: Relational systems increasingly support XML/JSON querying and indexing.
model_convergence.document_direction: Document systems increasingly add joins or database-reference resolution.
model_convergence.conclusion: Relational and document models complement each other, so hybrid systems supporting both are a useful direction.

imperative.definition: Tell the computer which operations to perform and in what order.
imperative.example: Loop through animals and append sharks to an output list.

declarative.definition: Specify the pattern/conditions of the desired result and let the system choose how to execute the query.

benefits_of_declarative: Allows the optimizer to change indexes/join algorithms/execution order without changing application queries.
Provides more freedom for parallel execution.

declarative_web_analogy.css: li.selected > p declares which elements should receive a style.
declarative_web_analogy.xpath_xsl: XPath/XSL similarly declare matching document patterns.
declarative_web_analogy.imperative_js_problem: DOM-manipulation code is longer, must explicitly undo prior state, and must be rewritten to exploit newer traversal APIs.
declarative_web_analogy.lesson: Declarative systems can automatically react to changing data/state and allow the implementation to be optimized independently.

mapreduce.definition: A bulk data-processing programming model popularized by Google for execution across many machines.
mapreduce.position_on_spectrum: Between declarative and fully imperative querying.

functions.map: Runs once per matching input document and emits key-value pairs.
functions.reduce: Runs for each grouped key and combines its values.

mapreduce.why_purity_matters: The framework can run functions anywhere, in any order, and rerun them after failure.
limitations: Requires coordinated map and reduce functions.
Provides fewer optimization opportunities than a declarative query.
mapreduce.mongodb_aggregation_pipeline: MongoDB added a more declarative aggregation pipeline, similar in expressiveness to a subset of SQL.

graph_models.when_natural: When many-to-many relationships are common and connections among records become complex.

examples.social_graph: People as vertices, relationships as edges.
examples.web_graph: Web pages as vertices, hyperlinks as edges.
examples.road_rail: Junctions as vertices, roads/rail lines as edges.

graph_models.heterogeneous_graph: A graph may contain different kinds of vertices and edges in the same model, such as people, places, events, check-ins, and comments.

important_properties: Any vertex can connect to any other vertex.
Incoming and outgoing traversal can be efficient.
Relationship labels allow many types of information in one graph.
property_graph.evolvability: Graphs are easy to extend with new vertex and edge types as application requirements change.

cypher.definition: Declarative property-graph query language created for Neo4j.
cypher.pattern_query: MATCH can express relationships such as a person born somewhere recursively WITHIN the United States and living somewhere recursively WITHIN Europe.
cypher.variable_length_path: :WITHIN*0.. means follow WITHIN zero or more times.
cypher.optimizer: Because Cypher is declarative, execution direction/order can be chosen by the query optimizer.

graph_queries_in_sql.challenge: Graph traversals may require an unknown number of edges/joins, whereas ordinary SQL queries usually specify a fixed number of joins.
graph_queries_in_sql.solution: Recursive common table expressions using WITH RECURSIVE, available since SQL:1999.
graph_queries_in_sql.tradeoff: Possible in SQL, but the example is much more verbose than Cypher.
graph_queries_in_sql.lesson: Different data models/query languages are optimized for different use cases.

triple_stores.subject: Equivalent to a graph vertex.
object_cases: Primitive value: predicate/object act like a property key/value.
Another vertex: predicate acts like an edge label between subject and object vertices.
triple_stores.turtle: Human-readable triple representation based on Notation3.

rdf_and_semantic_web.semantic_web_idea: Publish machine-readable data alongside human-readable web content so information from sites can be combined.
rdf_and_semantic_web.rdf: Resource Description Framework; a consistent data model for publishing and combining web data.
rdf_and_semantic_web.chapter_assessment: The semantic web was overhyped and has not been realized as originally envisioned, but useful ideas and tools emerged from it.
rdf_and_semantic_web.uri_namespaces: RDF often uses URIs for subjects/predicates/objects so independently created vocabularies do not collide.

sparql.definition: SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language for triple-stores using RDF.
sparql.relationship_to_cypher: Cypher's pattern matching is influenced by SPARQL and the syntax is conceptually similar.
sparql.strength: Concise declarative graph-pattern querying, including path expressions.

differences: Graph DB: any vertex can connect to any other; CODASYL schema restricts nesting/relationships.
Graph DB: vertices can be addressed directly by ID or index; CODASYL requires traversal through access paths.
Graph DB: vertices/edges are unordered; CODASYL children are ordered sets.
Graph DB: usually supports declarative languages; CODASYL queries were imperative.

datalog.history: Studied extensively by academics in the 1980s and foundational to later query-language ideas.
datalog.model: Generalizes triples by writing predicate(subject, object).
datalog.facts: Stored base assertions such as within(idaho, usa).
datalog.rules: Rules derive new predicates from stored facts or other rules; rules may call other rules recursively.
datalog.syntax: A rule applies when all predicates on the right side of :- match; the left side is then derived.
datalog.strength: Complex logic can be built incrementally from reusable rules.
datalog.tradeoff: Less convenient for simple one-off queries, but powerful for complex data.

chapter_conclusion.document: Best suited to self-contained documents with few inter-document relationships.
chapter_conclusion.relational: Strong general-purpose choice for structured data with joins and many-to-one/many-to-many relationships.
chapter_conclusion.graph: Best suited to heavily interconnected data where almost anything may relate to anything.
chapter_conclusion.schema_note: Document and graph databases often do not enforce schema, but the application still normally assumes a structure; the distinction is whether it is explicit on write or implicit on read.
specialized_models: Genome sequence-similarity databases such as GenBank

flashcards.front: Why are data models so important?
flashcards.back: They affect both how software is written and how engineers think about the problem.

flashcards.front: What is the first data-model layer?
flashcards.back: Represent real-world concepts as application-specific objects/data structures and APIs.

flashcards.front: What is the second data-model layer?
flashcards.back: Represent application structures using general-purpose models such as documents, relations, or graphs.

flashcards.front: What is the third data-model layer?
flashcards.back: Database software represents those models as bytes in memory, on disk, or on a network.

flashcards.front: What do data-model layers provide?
flashcards.back: Abstractions that hide lower-level complexity.

flashcards.front: Why is data-model choice important?
flashcards.back: Every model makes some uses easy and others awkward, slow, or unsupported.

flashcards.front: Who proposed the relational model?
flashcards.back: Edgar Codd in 1970.

flashcards.front: What is a relation in SQL terminology?
flashcards.back: A table: an unordered collection of tuples/rows.

flashcards.front: What was a major goal of the relational model?
flashcards.back: Hide internal storage representation behind a cleaner interface.

flashcards.front: When did relational databases become dominant?
flashcards.back: By the mid-1980s.

flashcards.front: What did NoSQL originally mean?
flashcards.back: A catchy Twitter hashtag for a 2009 meetup on open-source distributed nonrelational databases.

flashcards.front: What was NoSQL later reinterpreted as?
flashcards.back: Not Only SQL.

flashcards.front: Name four NoSQL adoption drivers.
flashcards.back: Scale/write throughput, open source, specialized queries, schema flexibility.

flashcards.front: What is polyglot persistence?
flashcards.back: Using relational and nonrelational datastores together because different use cases need different tools.

flashcards.front: What is object-relational impedance mismatch?
flashcards.back: The awkward mapping between object-oriented structures and relational tables/rows/columns.

flashcards.front: Name two ORM examples.
flashcards.back: ActiveRecord and Hibernate.

flashcards.front: Can ORMs completely hide relational/object differences?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: How are repeated résumé items traditionally normalized?
flashcards.back: Separate positions/education/contact tables with foreign keys to users.

flashcards.front: Why can a résumé fit a JSON document well?
flashcards.back: It is mostly a self-contained tree of one-to-many relationships.

flashcards.front: What locality advantage does JSON have for the résumé?
flashcards.back: All profile information can be fetched together in one query.

flashcards.front: What structure do one-to-many relationships naturally form?
flashcards.back: A tree.

flashcards.front: Why store region_id instead of the text name directly?
flashcards.back: To normalize human-readable information and avoid duplication.

flashcards.front: Why are stable IDs useful?
flashcards.back: They need not change even when human-readable attributes change.

flashcards.front: What is normalization's core idea?
flashcards.back: Store a fact once and refer to it, avoiding duplicated values.

flashcards.front: What consistency risk comes from duplicated human-readable data?
flashcards.back: Some copies may be updated while others remain stale.

flashcards.front: Why do normalized references challenge document databases?
flashcards.back: They create many-to-one relationships requiring joins or application-level lookups.

flashcards.front: What happens if a document DB lacks joins?
flashcards.back: Application code must emulate joins using multiple queries.

flashcards.front: How can added features make document data more interconnected?
flashcards.back: Organizations, schools, recommendations, and users become referenced entities.

flashcards.front: What historical database resembles modern nested documents?
flashcards.back: IBM IMS's hierarchical model.

flashcards.front: When was IMS commercially released?
What is the hierarchical model's key structural rule?
flashcards.back: Each record has exactly one parent.

flashcards.front: What relationship shape does the hierarchical model handle well?
flashcards.back: One-to-many.

flashcards.front: What relationship shape does it handle poorly?
flashcards.back: Many-to-many.

flashcards.front: What is CODASYL's network model?
flashcards.back: A generalization of the hierarchical model allowing records to have multiple parents.

flashcards.front: What is an access path in CODASYL?
flashcards.back: A predefined navigation path through pointer-like links among records.

flashcards.front: How were CODASYL queries performed?
flashcards.back: Imperatively, by moving a cursor and following access paths.

flashcards.front: Why were CODASYL access paths inflexible?
flashcards.back: Changing them could require rewriting application query code.

flashcards.front: How does the relational model differ from CODASYL navigation?
flashcards.back: Applications declare what data they need; the optimizer chooses access paths.

flashcards.front: Who chooses indexes and join order in a relational DB?
flashcards.back: The query optimizer.

flashcards.front: Why is a reusable optimizer valuable?
flashcards.back: It is built once and benefits all applications using the database.

flashcards.front: What are the main document-model advantages?
flashcards.back: Schema flexibility, locality, and a close match to tree-shaped application data.

flashcards.front: What are the main relational-model advantages?
flashcards.back: Joins and support for many-to-one/many-to-many relationships.

flashcards.front: When is a document model likely simpler?
flashcards.back: When the data is tree-shaped and usually loaded as a whole.

flashcards.front: When does document modeling become awkward?
flashcards.back: When data is highly interconnected or requires many-to-many relationships.

flashcards.front: What is one way to avoid document joins?
flashcards.back: Denormalization.

flashcards.front: What cost comes with denormalization?
flashcards.back: Application code must keep redundant data consistent.

flashcards.front: What is schema-on-read?
flashcards.back: Schema is implicit and interpreted when data is read.

flashcards.front: What is schema-on-write?
flashcards.back: Schema is explicit and enforced when data is written.

flashcards.front: What programming-language analogy is used for schema-on-read?
flashcards.back: Dynamic/runtime type checking.

flashcards.front: What programming-language analogy is used for schema-on-write?
flashcards.back: Static/compile-time type checking.

flashcards.front: How can a document model evolve from name to first_name?
flashcards.back: Start writing the new fields and handle old documents at read time.

flashcards.front: How does a relational schema typically evolve for the same change?
flashcards.back: ALTER TABLE, followed by UPDATE or read-time fallback.

flashcards.front: Is ALTER TABLE always slow?
flashcards.back: No; many relational databases execute simple ALTER TABLE quickly, though some cases/databases differ.

flashcards.front: What operation is likely slow on a large table?
flashcards.back: UPDATE rewriting every row.

flashcards.front: When is schema-on-read advantageous?
flashcards.back: Heterogeneous records or externally controlled structures that may change.

flashcards.front: When is an explicit schema useful?
flashcards.back: When records should have the same structure and enforcement/documentation is valuable.

flashcards.front: What is document locality?
flashcards.back: Related data is physically stored together in one encoded document.

flashcards.front: When does locality help?
flashcards.back: When the application reads most or all of the document together.

flashcards.front: When can locality hurt?
flashcards.back: When only a small field is needed from a large document.

flashcards.front: What update cost can documents have?
flashcards.back: The entire document often needs rewriting.

flashcards.front: What document-sizing guidance is given?
flashcards.back: Keep documents fairly small and avoid growth-heavy writes.

flashcards.front: Is locality unique to document DBs?
flashcards.back: No; Spanner, Oracle, and Bigtable-style models can also provide locality.

flashcards.front: How are relational and document databases converging?
flashcards.back: Relational systems add JSON/XML support while document systems add join-like features.

flashcards.front: What is an imperative query?
flashcards.back: A sequence of operations describing how to compute the result.

flashcards.front: What is a declarative query?
flashcards.back: A description of what result is wanted, leaving execution strategy to the system.

flashcards.front: What is the SQL shark example?
flashcards.back: SELECT * FROM animals WHERE family = 'Sharks';

flashcards.front: Why are declarative queries concise?
flashcards.back: They describe desired result conditions instead of step-by-step execution.

flashcards.front: Why do declarative queries aid optimization?
flashcards.back: The engine can change indexes, joins, order, or execution strategy without changing the query.

flashcards.front: Why can declarative queries parallelize more easily?
flashcards.back: They do not prescribe a fixed instruction sequence.

flashcards.front: What web language is used as a declarative analogy?
flashcards.back: CSS.

flashcards.front: What other declarative web technology is compared?
flashcards.back: XSL/XPath.

flashcards.front: Why is imperative DOM styling brittle?
flashcards.back: It must manually update/undo state and may need rewriting for new APIs.

flashcards.front: What is MapReduce?
flashcards.back: A bulk data-processing programming model for distributed execution across many machines.

flashcards.front: Is MapReduce fully declarative?
flashcards.back: No; it sits between declarative and fully imperative models.

flashcards.front: What does map do?
flashcards.back: Runs on each input and emits key-value pairs.

flashcards.front: What does reduce do?
flashcards.back: Combines values grouped under the same key.

flashcards.front: What does the shark example reduce to?
flashcards.back: 3 + 4 = 7 sharks for December 1995.

flashcards.front: What does purity mean for map/reduce functions?
flashcards.back: They only use inputs, make no extra DB queries, and have no side effects.

flashcards.front: Why are pure functions useful for distributed execution?
flashcards.back: They can run anywhere, in any order, and be rerun after failure.

flashcards.front: What MapReduce usability issue is described?
flashcards.back: Two coordinated functions are harder than one declarative query.

flashcards.front: What did MongoDB add in 2.2?
flashcards.back: The declarative aggregation pipeline.

flashcards.front: When is a graph model natural?
flashcards.back: When many-to-many relationships are pervasive and data is highly interconnected.

flashcards.front: What are a graph's two core object types?
flashcards.back: Vertices and edges.

flashcards.front: What are vertices also called?
flashcards.back: Nodes or entities.

flashcards.front: What are edges also called?
flashcards.back: Relationships or arcs.

flashcards.front: Give three graph examples.
flashcards.back: Social graph, web graph, road/rail network.

flashcards.front: Can graph vertices be heterogeneous?
flashcards.back: Yes; one graph can contain people, places, events, comments, etc.

flashcards.front: What fields does a property-graph vertex have?
flashcards.back: ID, incoming edges, outgoing edges, and key-value properties.

flashcards.front: What fields does a property-graph edge have?
flashcards.back: ID, tail, head, label, and key-value properties.

flashcards.front: What graph property improves evolvability?
flashcards.back: Any vertex may connect to any other without rigid relationship restrictions.

flashcards.front: What is Cypher?
flashcards.back: A declarative query language for property graphs, created for Neo4j.

flashcards.front: What does (Idaho)-[:WITHIN]->(USA) mean?
flashcards.back: An edge labeled WITHIN from Idaho to USA.

flashcards.front: What does :WITHIN*0.. mean?
flashcards.back: Follow a WITHIN edge zero or more times.

flashcards.front: Why can Cypher choose different traversal strategies?
flashcards.back: It is declarative and the optimizer chooses execution details.

flashcards.front: How can SQL express variable-length graph traversal?
flashcards.back: Recursive common table expressions using WITH RECURSIVE.

flashcards.front: Why is graph SQL often awkward?
flashcards.back: Graph traversals may require an unknown number of joins.

flashcards.front: What is a triple-store statement?
flashcards.back: (subject, predicate, object).

flashcards.front: What does a primitive object represent in a triple?
flashcards.back: A vertex property value.

flashcards.front: What does a vertex object represent in a triple?
flashcards.back: An edge from the subject to another vertex.

flashcards.front: What is Turtle?
flashcards.back: A human-readable syntax for triples/RDF.

flashcards.front: What is the semantic web idea?
flashcards.back: Publish machine-readable structured data across websites so it can be combined.

flashcards.front: What is RDF?
flashcards.back: Resource Description Framework.

flashcards.front: Why does RDF use URI namespaces?
flashcards.back: To prevent vocabulary/name collisions when data from different sources is combined.

flashcards.front: What is SPARQL?
flashcards.back: A declarative query language for RDF triple-stores.

flashcards.front: How are SPARQL and Cypher related?
flashcards.back: Both use similar graph-pattern matching; Cypher borrowed ideas from SPARQL.

flashcards.front: Are graph databases simply CODASYL reborn?
flashcards.back: No; graph DBs differ in flexibility, direct access, ordering, and query languages.

flashcards.front: What is Datalog?
flashcards.back: A logic/declarative query language foundational to later query-language ideas.

flashcards.front: How does Datalog write a triple-like fact?
flashcards.back: predicate(subject, object).

flashcards.front: What is a Datalog rule?
flashcards.back: A derivation that creates a new predicate when predicates on the right side match.

flashcards.front: Can Datalog rules be recursive?
flashcards.back: Yes.

flashcards.front: What is Datalog good at?
flashcards.back: Building complex queries incrementally from reusable rules.

flashcards.front: What is Datalog less convenient for?
flashcards.back: Simple one-off queries.

flashcards.front: What use case do document DBs target in the summary?
flashcards.back: Self-contained documents with rare relationships between documents.

flashcards.front: What use case do graph DBs target?
flashcards.back: Highly interconnected data where anything may relate to anything.

flashcards.front: Can one model emulate another?
flashcards.back: Yes, but the result is often awkward.

flashcards.front: What query languages/frameworks are summarized?
flashcards.back: SQL, MapReduce, MongoDB aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL, Datalog.

scenario_questions.scenario: A user profile contains name, a list of jobs, a list of schools, and contact information and is almost always loaded in full.
scenario_questions.question: Which data model has a natural fit?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A document model, because the structure is a self-contained tree of one-to-many relationships with good locality.

scenario_questions.scenario: The profile system adds company pages, school pages, recommendations, and references between users.
scenario_questions.question: How does this change the data-model tradeoff?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The data becomes more interconnected with many-to-one/many-to-many relationships, making joins/references more important and the relational or graph model more attractive.

scenario_questions.scenario: Every profile stores 'Greater Seattle Area' as a string. The city name must now change.
scenario_questions.question: What normalization issue appears?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The human-readable value is duplicated. Using a stable region ID would allow the name to be updated once.

scenario_questions.scenario: A database forces application code to walk pointer paths to reach records, and a schema change requires rewriting traversal code.
scenario_questions.question: Which historical model does this resemble?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: CODASYL/network model with application-managed access paths.

scenario_questions.scenario: You add a new database index and existing SQL queries get faster without code changes.
scenario_questions.question: What design advantage does this demonstrate?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Declarative relational queries separate what is requested from the access path, allowing the query optimizer to adopt the new index automatically.

scenario_questions.scenario: Incoming records have different structures because third-party providers evolve independently.
scenario_questions.question: Which schema style may be advantageous?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Schema-on-read, because heterogeneous externally controlled data can be handled by read-time logic.

scenario_questions.scenario: Every record is expected to contain the same required fields and invalid shapes should be rejected immediately.
scenario_questions.question: Which schema style is attractive?

scenario_questions.scenario: A 5 MB document is read frequently, but only a 30-byte status field is needed.
scenario_questions.question: What document-locality limitation applies?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The database may need to load the entire document, wasting I/O for a tiny partial read.

scenario_questions.scenario: A query specifies only filtering/grouping conditions, while the database chooses indexes and execution order.
scenario_questions.question: What query style is this?

scenario_questions.scenario: A CSS rule automatically stops applying when an element's class changes.
scenario_questions.question: What database-query concept does the chapter use this to illustrate?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Declarative specifications let the underlying system manage execution/state changes without imperative application code.

scenario_questions.scenario: You need distributed aggregation where tasks can be retried on arbitrary workers after failures.
scenario_questions.question: What MapReduce restriction helps?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Map and reduce functions are pure: input-only, no extra database queries, and no side effects.

scenario_questions.scenario: Your records form a social network in which people, events, locations, and comments can all connect in many ways.
scenario_questions.question: What data model is most natural?

scenario_questions.scenario: A query needs to follow 'within' relationships through an unknown number of geographic levels.
scenario_questions.question: How do Cypher and SQL express this?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Cypher uses a variable-length path such as :WITHIN*0..; SQL can use recursive CTEs with WITH RECURSIVE, but more verbosely.

scenario_questions.scenario: You need to express 'Lucy marriedTo Alain' using a triple-store.
scenario_questions.question: What is the triple?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: (lucy, marriedTo, alain), where marriedTo is the predicate/edge.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two organizations both define a predicate called 'within' with different meanings.
scenario_questions.question: How does RDF avoid collision?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Use distinct URI namespaces so the predicates have globally distinguishable identifiers.

scenario_questions.scenario: A graph query requires reusable recursive rules about geographic containment and migration.
scenario_questions.question: Which language in the chapter is especially suited?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Datalog, because rules can derive predicates recursively and be composed/reused.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with layers of data models?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: To show that software continually translates one representation into another, and each layer provides an abstraction that hides lower-level complexity.

short_answer_questions.question: Why did NoSQL emerge despite relational database dominance?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Different applications needed greater scale/write throughput, open-source options, specialized queries, and more flexible data models, so nonrelational systems complemented rather than simply replaced relational systems.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can a résumé be easier to model as JSON than normalized SQL?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It is primarily a self-contained one-to-many tree. JSON mirrors the application structure and gives good locality, whereas normalized SQL splits the tree across multiple tables.

short_answer_questions.question: What does normalization buy you?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It stores human-meaningful information once behind stable IDs, reducing duplicated writes and the risk that copies become inconsistent.

short_answer_questions.question: Why do document databases become less attractive as applications mature?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Features often introduce more references and many-to-many relationships, which require joins or application-level lookup/consistency logic.

short_answer_questions.question: What was the relational model's major improvement over CODASYL?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It removed application-visible access-path navigation. Queries declare desired data and a reusable optimizer chooses indexes, joins, and execution order.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare schema-on-read and schema-on-write.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Schema-on-read leaves structure implicit and handles compatibility in read code; schema-on-write makes structure explicit and validates writes. The choice depends on heterogeneity and desired enforcement.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the locality tradeoff in document databases?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Co-located data can make whole-document reads efficient, but partial reads can waste I/O and updates may require rewriting the whole document.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are declarative query languages powerful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They describe desired results rather than execution steps, allowing the engine to optimize indexes, join strategies, storage layout, and parallel execution independently of application code.

short_answer_questions.question: Why must MapReduce functions be pure?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Purity allows tasks to be moved, reordered, and retried across workers without changing semantics.

short_answer_questions.question: When should you consider a graph model?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: When many-to-many relationships dominate and the application needs to traverse complex, evolving connections among heterogeneous entities.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can Cypher be clearer than SQL for graph traversal?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Cypher directly expresses variable-length relationship patterns, while SQL often requires recursive CTEs and much more verbose join logic.

short_answer_questions.question: How are property graphs and triple-stores related?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Both represent entities and relationships. In triples, primitive objects correspond to properties and vertex objects correspond to edges.

short_answer_questions.question: How is a modern graph database different from CODASYL?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Graphs allow arbitrary links, direct ID/index access, unordered vertices/edges, and declarative queries, whereas CODASYL imposed schema-defined paths, ordered children, and imperative navigation.

short_answer_questions.question: What makes Datalog powerful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Complex predicates can be built incrementally from reusable and recursive rules, which is useful when data relationships and reasoning become complex.

common_confusions.correction: The term was a meetup hashtag and was later reinterpreted as 'Not Only SQL'; the chapter expects relational and nonrelational systems to coexist.

common_confusions.confusion: Schemaless means the data has no structure.
common_confusions.correction: Application code still assumes structure; the schema is implicit and interpreted on read rather than enforced by the database on write.

common_confusions.confusion: Document databases eliminate all joins forever.
common_confusions.correction: As data becomes interconnected, references and many-to-many relationships appear; joins may be emulated in application code or supported by the database.

common_confusions.confusion: Normalization is only about saving storage.
common_confusions.correction: It reduces duplicated human-meaningful information, simplifies updates, and reduces inconsistency risk.
It helps whole-document reads but can waste I/O on partial reads and force larger rewrites.

common_confusions.confusion: Relational databases cannot store JSON-like data.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter notes significant XML/JSON support in relational systems and predicts increasing convergence.

common_confusions.confusion: Declarative SQL is less powerful because it hides execution details.
common_confusions.correction: Hiding execution details gives the optimizer freedom to improve plans and parallel execution without query changes.

common_confusions.confusion: MapReduce and SQL are opposites where SQL cannot be distributed.
common_confusions.correction: SQL can run on distributed systems; MapReduce does not have a monopoly on distributed query execution.

common_confusions.confusion: A graph database is just CODASYL with a modern name.
common_confusions.correction: Graph DBs allow arbitrary edges, direct vertex lookup, unordered relationships, and declarative query languages.

common_confusions.confusion: RDF requires buying into the semantic web vision.
common_confusions.correction: Triple/RDF models can be useful internally even if the semantic web never becomes an internet-wide database.

practice_problems.prompt: You are building a CMS where each article contains nested sections and comments, and articles rarely reference one another. Which model is a natural starting point?
practice_problems.solution: Document model, because data is largely self-contained and tree-shaped.

practice_problems.prompt: You are building a professional network with companies, schools, people, recommendations, memberships, and many cross-links. Which models become more attractive?
practice_problems.solution: Relational for structured joins, or graph when relationships become deeply interconnected.

practice_problems.prompt: 10 million profiles duplicate the same industry name. The industry is renamed. What modeling choice reduces update risk?
practice_problems.solution: Store one industry entity keyed by a stable ID and reference that ID from profiles.

practice_problems.prompt: Old user documents contain name while new documents contain first_name. What schema-on-read pattern can handle both?
practice_problems.solution: At read time, if first_name is absent but name exists, derive first_name from the old field.

practice_problems.prompt: An application always renders a whole product document in one request. What document-model advantage matters?
practice_problems.solution: Data locality: the related content can be fetched together without multiple index lookups/joins.

practice_problems.prompt: Why can changing a database index speed up SQL without changing the query?
practice_problems.solution: SQL is declarative; the optimizer can choose a new access path/index while preserving the same logical query.

practice_problems.prompt: Map emits ('2026-08', 2), ('2026-08', 5), ('2026-08', 4). If reduce sums values, what is the result?
You need to follow an unknown number of 'manager-of' or 'within' relationships. Why is a graph query language attractive?
practice_problems.solution: Variable-length path expressions represent recursive traversal directly, instead of manually fixing a join depth.

practice_problems.prompt: Convert vertex property Lucy.age=33 into triple form.
If within(idaho, usa) and within(usa, namerica), what kind of Datalog mechanism can derive that Idaho is within North America?
practice_problems.solution: A recursive containment rule such as within_recursive.

must_memorize: Data models shape both code and thought.
Layers: real world -> application structures -> documents/tables/graphs -> bytes -> hardware.
Relational model: Codd 1970; tables are unordered collections of rows.
NoSQL drivers: scale, open source, specialized queries, schema flexibility.
Polyglot persistence = multiple database paradigms coexist.
Object-relational impedance mismatch persists even with ORMs.
Document model fits self-contained one-to-many trees and offers locality.
Normalization uses stable IDs to avoid duplicated human-readable facts.
Many-to-one/many-to-many relationships favor joins/references.
IMS = hierarchical one-parent tree.
CODASYL = multiple parents + pointer-like application-managed access paths.
Relational optimizer chooses access paths, indexes, join order.
Document strengths: schema flexibility/locality/tree mapping.
Relational strengths: joins and connected structured relationships.
Schema-on-read = implicit/read-time; schema-on-write = explicit/write-time.
Document locality helps whole-document reads but hurts large partial reads/rewrites.
Relational and document databases are converging.
Imperative = how; declarative = what.
Declarative queries create optimizer and parallelization freedom.
MapReduce: map emits key-values; reduce combines by key; functions must be pure.
Graph = vertices + edges; ideal for dense many-to-many relationships.
Property graph edges have tail, head, label, properties.
Cypher supports variable-length paths such as *0...
SQL recursive CTEs can perform graph traversal but are verbose.
Triple-store = subject-predicate-object.
RDF uses URI namespaces; SPARQL queries RDF graphs.
Modern graph DBs are not CODASYL.
Datalog = facts + reusable/recursive rules.
No one model is universally best.
final_review.memory_chain: LAYERS -> RELATIONAL -> NOSQL -> OBJECT/RELATIONAL MISMATCH -> JSON TREE -> NORMALIZATION -> MANY-TO-MANY -> IMS/CODASYL -> QUERY OPTIMIZER -> DOCUMENT vs RELATIONAL -> SCHEMA-ON-READ/WRITE -> LOCALITY -> DECLARATIVE SQL -> CSS/XPATH -> MAPREDUCE -> GRAPH -> PROPERTY GRAPH -> CYPHER -> RECURSIVE SQL -> TRIPLES/RDF -> SPARQL -> DATALOG
final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Choose a data model based on the shape of relationships and access patterns: documents excel at self-contained trees, relations at structured joins, and graphs at dense connectivity, while declarative query languages give the system freedom to optimize how those models are traversed.
